translations.text: The life and conduct of Saint Jacob, who was made bishop in the city of Nisibis. Moses, the great prophet,
who parted the Red Sea and led the children of Israel through on dry land, and brought forth water for them in the waterless desert from a dry rock, and satisfied that people of myriads,
and went up Mount Sinai to bring down for them the book of the Law.
And before he came down, that people became godless. And they made themselves an idol and worshipped it.
This prophet did none of all this of himself, but by the mercy of God which descended upon him;
through it he was able to do all this. And how could I be able to open my mouth and move my tongue to speak,
except that, trusting in that holy power and by its help, I move my tongue and speak of the virtues of Abel and the love of God of Enoch and the righteousness of Noah and
the priesthood of Melchizedek in holiness and the faith of Abraham and his patience and hospitality and his many offerings and his virtues,
the patience of Job in the things that befell him, his thanksgiving and that love of his toward strangers, and his freedom from anger toward the poor.
And further, I intend to narrate the life of this saint and the miraculous deeds of this holy man, and I ask the help of God, that he may give me power to write it down in truth and righteousness.
And I wish this Life to be in a worthy and fitting place, so that all who read it may be eager to imitate the deeds of this saint.
And now, through his prayer, I ask mercy from God and I begin to narrate his life.
The city of Nisibis lies on the border of Persia and of the Greeks.
And formerly the kings of the Greeks collected its tribute, for it was under their authority.
There was in this city a certain man, a monk, whose name was Jacob. And from his youth he had taken the yoke of monasticism upon his neck.
And he lived in remote deserts and dwelt in seclusion on the tops of mountains. And in the heat of summer he burned himself under the sun.
He would not go under a roof for shade from the sun, and in the days of winter he stayed in a very narrow cave, in which he could not stand upright.
And his food was not of wheat or barley, or of anything else that is produced by the labor of hands,
but he fed on the wild herbs of the desert and on the fruits of wild trees,
on which no man had labored and which no one had watered; from these came the sustenance of his body, after God.
And his clothing was woven of goat hair, and his wrap was one small piece of coarse haircloth.
And he greatly constrained himself, struck down and subdued his mind,
for he lived like an angel on earth. And the sight of him was to the glory of God, as the Apostle says,
and at all times his appearance was changed from glory to glory, and he was joyful, and his speech was the glory of God.
And by the gentleness of his heart he gained great boldness before God, so that every request,
Whatever he asked of God was given to him immediately and without hindrance, at all times.
He entreated God humbly and asked for what it is proper to ask of God, namely forgiveness and remission of sins,
the mercy and grace of God had come down upon him, and he taught them the way of truth, and they did not heed his teaching.
Then he derided them and rebuked them for the thing by which the devil had corrupted [?] their minds: they had abandoned the Creator and served created things.
At that time divine zeal was kindled in the heart of this saint, like that of the prophet Elijah, when he saw people in the perdition of idol-worship, as Elijah had seen the Israelites.
He came down from the mountain where he had settled and set out for Persia, in order to visit that planting of Christianity,
to pray for them, teach them and strengthen them in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they might not turn from truth to falsehood and perish forever.
And when he reached the gate of a certain city called Beida, which was within the borders of Persia,
there was at the gate of this city a spring welling up, from which the city drew its life. And a monk was passing by the gate of that city and saw
many women at that spring, washing their clothes and treading them with their feet, having shamelessly hitched up their garments.
And when those women saw the monk, not only did they not cover their heads and shins with their garments, but they began to laugh loudly, and they mocked and reproached him.
They felt no shame before him as an old man, nor did they show reverence for the venerable monastic habit that the holy elder wore,
but they looked at him with shameless eyes and shouted at him with ugly and disgraceful words, laughing at him foully and senselessly.
Then, when the holy elder saw them in such shamelessness and wantonness and heard what they were shouting at him, he was greatly grieved for them.
And he wished to show a miracle upon them by the power of God, in order to turn them back from such impudence [?] and shamelessness.

And he cursed the spring, and immediately it dried up. Then he made the sign of the cross over those women, and immediately the whiteness of their faces turned black and became like a raven's feathers.
And the blackness of their hair turned white and became white as snow.
And their features became like a fig leaf when frost has struck it, and so dreadful and terrible was the sight of them.
Then, when those women saw one another's faces and hair, how in an instant they had become a disgrace, and that the spring had dried up, they hurried
and went into the city and told the citizens all that had happened.
And they gathered at once and came out to look for that monk, and they pursued him eagerly.
And they overtook him, for they had passed beyond that city.
And when they overtook him, they all fell down before the wondrous elder, bowing low and kissing his feet, so that by this they might somehow assuage his anger.
But when the elder saw them, he took pity on them, for they were weeping before him with such tears and saying:
"O holy father, the life of this city comes from this spring, upon which it is built;
and if it dries up, all these souls will perish of thirst and the city will be laid waste.
But have mercy on this countless multitude, and let us not perish through the foolishness of these women,
who are reaping the fruit of their insolence; and do not exact their sin from this people, who have committed no sin against you."
Then the holy man turned back there to the head of the spring, lifted up his hands to heaven, prayed to God, and said:
"Lord, do not hold their foolishness against them, but forgive them, and command this spring again to gush forth abundantly,
as it did before and more than that, so that they may believe in your holy name and confess you, the only good God."
And at once the spring gushed forth again, far more than before, as if from a great deep.
And when the citizens saw this miracle, they kissed his feet with weeping and begged him to pray for the women as well, so that they might be restored as before.
Now all these citizens had been turned by the devil from Christianity to paganism.
And the elder commanded them to abandon the law of paganism, to serve Christ our God, and to build churches.
Then they eagerly accepted the elder's teaching because of the miracles they had seen from him, and all of them went with him and looked for a place for a church.
And when they had found a place, they at once built a church with great zeal, and all of them turned back with joy and became Christians.
He chose and appointed priests and deacons for them. Again they entreated him for the healing of the women, and he commanded them
to bring them to him, so that he might lay down a rule for them no longer to dare such shamelessness, but to walk in humility and to conduct themselves with [?] and modestly, as is fitting for women.
But they did not come to him, out of shame, and he left them as they were, for the good of their souls. And in purity before them, the doorkeepers would not dare to hinder him [?].
So too with this holy man: everything he wanted from God, God gave him without hindrance.
After this he was going out by the gates of a certain city, and he saw beggars gathered together, asking for alms.
And when they saw him coming from a distance, they immediately got up, stretched out one of their companions on the ground, and covered him with a sheet like a dead man.
And when he reached them, they begged the elder to perform the prayer for the dead over him so that they might bury him. And the holy man granted their request and
stood facing east and entreated God to forgive the man his sins and to number him among the saints in the kingdom of heaven.
And when he had entreated Christ for the soul of the man who was reckoned as dead, though he was alive,
Christ accepted the elder's prayer, brought that soul out of the body, and led it away to the kingdom for which the holy man had been entreating;
he fulfilled his request and did not disregard it. Although that soul had not left the body, through the elder's prayer he brought it out and led it away to heaven.
And when the elder had finished his prayer over him, he told them to bury him, and he himself set off on his way.
And when he had gone some distance from them, the dead man's companions began, with laughter and mockery, to call to him to get up, so that they might go on their way together.
And when they had called him many times and there was no response, they supposed that he had fallen asleep.
And one of them went to wake him, and when he lifted the sheet from his face, he saw the color of earth on his face.
At once he put his hand to his nostrils and found that he had grown cold and that the breath had ceased from his nose.
And when he saw that life had departed from him, he at once told his companions, "This man is dead."
And when all the others heard this, they immediately ran after the holy man, overtook him, fell down before him, kissed his hands and feet, and with weeping humbly begged him
to forgive them the foolishness that they had committed against him in the madness of their poverty; and they told him about their companion,
how he had stretched himself out [?] while alive and now they had found him dead, and they begged him to restore his soul to him again.
And the elder, when he heard these words from them, and because they were weeping before him,
had mercy on them and turned back with them, and he went and stood over the dead man, raised his hands to heaven, and prayed to God to restore the man's soul to his body.
And the soul that had departed from the man through the elder's prayer returned to his body through that same prayer.
And the dead man arose and began to chant [?] to his companions in great pain, and he said to them:
"May the Lord see and judge between me and you, for you have brought me out of the kingdom of heaven, of which I had been made worthy through the prayer of this holy man,
and you have returned me to this earth, full of falsehood and deceit, and have deprived me of those eternal good things, which I can no longer attain because of my unworthiness."
The holy man performed this miracle just as the apostle Peter did when Ananias and Sapphira his wife lied to him and he immediately caused them to die.
So too with this holy man: when those foolish men lied to him, God made their lie true.
But the Holy Spirit revealed their lie to Peter, and he caused them to die knowingly, whereas this holy elder in ignorance prayed over that man
as over a dead man, for he truly thought him dead; and Christ did not disregard his prayer and made him truly dead.
Let those who foolishly mock read this writing, and let them cease from their foolish mockery and repent!
From here on let us leave off speaking of this and pass on to his other miracles and virtues.
And let us speak briefly and not go on at length: Arius, that head of heresy, father of lies, and author of blasphemy,
who devised blasphemy against the only Son of God and the Holy Spirit, and sharpened his tongue like a cutting sword,
began with the cunning of falsehood to divide the one essence of the Trinity, and he filled all Egypt with turmoil and with the heresy of his deadly teaching, and made many sharers in his perdition,
until his blasphemies were heard throughout the whole world.
This was in the days of the faithful emperor Constantine, who was crowned with the crown of faith,
who turned back the captivity of that people of Israel, for the children of the temple of God were being slaughtered by the heathen in every place.
When the God-crowned emperor saw this turmoil and division [?] of the faith which the lawless Arius had stirred up, the emperor commanded
that all the high priests, the governors of the churches, should quickly assemble in the city of Nicaea, to settle that turmoil and heresy.
And when this became known to the holy monk Jacob, he too prepared to go up to Nicaea with the bishops,
in order to make manifest the law of the true faith, just as a brave warrior openly displays his courage in combat.
For the city of Nisibis was under the authority of the Greeks, and the Greek kings took its tribute.
And when this holy assembly gathered at Nicaea, the holy monk Jacob was also with them, and there was much disputation among them.
And with the crafty Arius, moreover, there were also many others, who followed him with words of falsehood, and those enemies of the truth inclined to his utterly evil will.
But they could not openly declare this before people, except only to those who shared with them in that craftiness.
They were full of all guile and of that deception of the devil, and secretly, like snakes, they bit people on the heel;
but the power of God and his mercy, which always protects his holy churches and all the faithful
who serve him in truth, did not neglect the children of the holy catholic church.
And with the crafty Arius there were seven evil leading elders, who lied his lie and shared in his will.
They were good in word and evil in mind, as the prophet says:
"This people glorifies me with their lips, but their hearts are far removed from me."
And again Jeremiah says: "Truly you are near to their mouth and far from their kidneys," as holy David says:
"With their mouth they blessed and with their heart they cursed." And again: "Their words were softer than oil, and they were like the points of arrows."
Such were those deceitful and wicked men, who tenderly entreated holy Alexander, patriarch of Alexandria,
to have mercy on Arius and release him from his ban. But holy Alexander was afraid of those wicked men and wished to bring their affair to a successful end.
For many others too had come in sincerity to help them, out of a better intention, and they too said to holy Alexander:
"Our God is a lover of mercy, and mercy toward a sinner gladdens him."
Holy Alexander answered them: "I tell you the truth, my children, that to show mercy to the accursed one, the crafty Arius, is an exceedingly great sin."
Then the holy bishop Jacob of the city of Nisibis, whose life I have recounted to you, counselled the holy assembly to fast for seven days and to stay without sleep all the nights,
to pass the night until dawn in prayer, and thus to entreat God that he act according to his will on behalf of his flock, the children of the church.
And when all the bishops heard this from Saint James, they accepted his counsel with joy, and they fasted for seven days and kept vigil seven nights.
And they fervently implored God to govern his flock according to his will, and, if Arius was worthy of forgiveness from him, to reveal it to them.
And the seventh day came, the Lord's day, on which they were expecting a sign to be revealed to them concerning the forgiveness and absolution of Arius.
And when it was the hour for offering the sacrifices of the mystery, the whole assembly lifted up their hands to God.
At that moment God showed a miracle by the power of his divinity upon the lawless Arius,
for the holy assembly summoned him so that, if he was worthy, they might have him share with them in the service of the liturgy.
And when he rose from his seat and went into the latrine to relieve the natural need that is laid upon us, at that very moment the power of God showed such a miracle upon him: all
that was in his belly, the intestines and the heart and liver together with the lungs, poured out through his anus, and he fell down in that foul place,
as he deserved, and he breathed out his spirit wretchedly, through the wrath from above and through the prayer of our holy father James, bishop of Nisibis,
who was stirred against him with divine zeal, like Phinehas the priest, who killed those two who were sinning, because of whom the people of God were being destroyed,
and their killing calmed the wrath of God and the death was stopped, as it is written in the book of the Psalms:
"Phinehas stood up and delivered them, and the death was stopped, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness from generation to generation and forever."
In the same way this saint killed that lawless and crafty, accursed Arius with a weapon from God,
for in his prayer to God his tongue became sharper than any two-edged sword.
And with it he killed that foul and crafty, accursed Arius and delivered the flock of Christ from his deadly and destructive poison, as it is written:
"Let the ungodly be destroyed, so that he may not see the glory of God."
After the death of the ungodly Arius this holy assembly dispersed, and each man went away to his own home with great joy.
And Saint James returned to his see in the city of Nisibis, like a valiant soldier
who has routed the enemy and expects to receive a crown from the king for his struggle.
And all people, whenever they heard his name, came out from the cities and from all the country to meet him on the road, so that they might be blessed by him.
And after a short time the great and faithful emperor Constantine fell asleep and was crowned with a heavenly crown in place of an earthly one.
And his sons inherited his empire after him.
And when Shapur, king of the Persians, heard that the emperor Constantine had died and that his sons had taken possession of his empire,
he grew arrogant in mind and made ready his army, in order to wage war on the Greeks and take their dominions from them by force.
And he laid siege to the city of Nisibis with a countless host, for it was the border of their dominion, and when he saw it enclosed by a strong wall,
He commanded his army to set up around it another, higher wall and to build on top of it a multitude of catapults for shooting at the city.
And he also made wagons fitted with machines, to bring them up against the wall and with them to tear out its foundation.
And when they had done all this and achieved nothing by it, because the prayer of Saint James prevailed over all the cunning of their machines,
and King Shapur saw that all their devices were in vain, he then commanded his host to block that river

which flowed into the city, and to dam it up and dig around the walls of the city, and, when the water had risen, to release it violently, so that it would strike their walls and they would be destroyed,
for that lawless man knew that its walls were of mud brick, and clay cannot stand against water.
And they did as King Shapur had commanded them: they dammed up the water and then released it all at once, and the water struck the walls of the city and surrounded it.
And the clay could not withstand the water, and it softened the foundation of the wall, and the walls of the city fell and were destroyed on every side.
When the inhabitants of the city saw this, that their walls had fallen,
terror fell upon them and unspeakable fear seized them, and they gave up hope for their lives and wished to surrender themselves to the king of the Persians as his slaves.
But Saint James, their true shepherd, who trusted in the power and goodness of God more than in the strength of walls, comforted them and said to them:
"Do not be afraid, my children, and do not tremble, for Christ our God will not give this city into the hands of the lawless king. Do not be afraid!"
Then, when Shapur king of the Persians saw that the walls of the city had fallen,
he rejoiced with great joy and commanded his host to enter from every side and seize the city.
And when the horsemen prepared to enter the city, they could not, because of the clay and mud that had been stirred up by the water,
for their mounts were sinking, and the foot soldiers and light troops were also going down into that mud.
And when they proved unable to enter on that day, he commanded them to withdraw a little,
until that pit of mud had dried out, and then to seize the city. When those who were

in the city saw all this that had happened, they raised their hands to heaven and prayed to God with contrite hearts, together with their shepherd Saint James, that they might be delivered from that calamity.
And all came out together, men and women and children, and began to build a wall on the inner side of that ruin, and with the help of God and the prayer of Saint James they built the wall of the city

on every side in a single night, higher and stronger than the first, and they set on top of it a man-headed [?] battlement, and they were strengthened in mind and comforted, and they besought Saint James,
their spiritual shepherd, to go up on that wall and curse the Persian host.
And when he went up to the height of the wall in order to curse them, and looked upon the countless multitude of the army that surrounded the city.
He took pity on them and remembered the word of the Apostle: "Bless those who curse you and do not curse," and he refrained from cursing that people.
Instead he prayed only this: that God would send upon them gnats and wasps [?], so that by this they might be scattered from that place and go away from there, and none of them be killed.
And God heard his prayer, as he had heard that of Moses the prophet, and at once this scourge from God came upon them through the prayer of holy Jacob.
And gnats came up out of the earth against them, upon the men, and wasps upon their horses, and quickly scattered them,
for they also had many elephants with them for battle, and the wasps were upon these too, until they became unable to stand before the wasps and the gnats.
And when that army had been scattered across the face of the land [?], Shapur, king of the Persians, saw

that the walls of the city had been built higher and stronger than before, and that his host was weakened for battle and scattered, and that all their skill had been made vain; and dread came over him and he was afraid.
He looked toward the wall and saw holy Jacob the bishop as he walked upon the walls.
He was clothed in his garment of sackcloth, and a cowl was on his head. And when King Shapur saw him, he thought that the king of the Greeks had come,
for by God's providence that garment of sackcloth appeared to his eyes as the king's purple, and the holy cowl as a crown.
And he said to his counselors and his intimates, who had advised him to come and fight against the city of Nisibis, saying that the king of the Greeks had died:
"Why did you deceive me, O wicked counselors, and tell me that the king was not here, and by this seek my death?
Behold, do I not see with my own eyes the king of the Greeks walking on the walls, with a crown on his head?
And our people have been scattered, and how shall we escape from death?
But before they come out of the city and slaughter us, I will take vengeance on you for your lie to me!"
And he commanded the soldiers to cut off the heads of all his counselors and magi and diviners.
And they did so. And he at once broke camp there in great fear and returned to his own land, and some of their armor
and equipment and tents they left behind out of fear. Such a miracle God worked through holy Jacob, as Hezekiah did.
And this is not less than that of Hezekiah, but greater and more, for those citizens had been given up as lost
when their walls fell, yet by the prayer of holy Jacob those enemies were driven away.
But I greatly marvel at the meekness of that man of God, how he did not curse those enemies, so that fire might come down and burn them up,
as Elijah the prophet did to those three captains of fifty, how he burned them up with fire from above; and he did not command the earth either
to open its mouth and swallow them, as Moses the prophet swallowed up Dathan and Abiram, who rose up against Moses.
Rather, he remembered the word of our Savior, which he said to the disciples James and John, the sons of Zebedee, when the Samaritans drove them away:
"Lord, let us speak, so that fire may come down and destroy them, as Elijah did":
But hear how the Lord said to them: "You do not know of what spirit you are."
And this saint likewise asked nothing of God by which he might have called down death and destruction upon them,
but only this insect and feeble plant, by means of which he drove those enemies away from his land in peace, and not one of them perished.
Such boldness before God had the blessed Jacob gained through his great ascetic struggle, so that God fulfilled every wish of his heart without delay.
And after this he left this transitory world and went before God to those eternal places of rest,
which are prepared for those who struggle and for those who have loved God with all their heart and with all their soul.
And there he took up his dwelling in the kingdom of heaven. But after this the Persians again grew stronger than the Greeks, and they took the city of Nisibis.
And the inhabitants of the city moved away from that place and carried with them the body of Saint Jacob the bishop, and those faithful people said:
"Let us not be under the authority of the pagans." And they came to the emperor of the Greeks, and the emperor gave them a city to live in.
And they built a very beautiful and splendid church, and they laid in it the body of Saint Jacob the bishop.
And through his intercession and prayer may the Lord grant his grace to us, to all faithful Christians,
by which we may be able to glorify the name of the Holy Trinity, to whom belongs glory, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
